title: Simple Cache
story: Your app computes Fibonacci numbers on demand — but computing fib(40) takes forever, and users keep asking for the same numbers. You need a cache: a way to remember answers you've already computed, so you only calculate each value once.
why: Caching is one of the most powerful performance optimizations — a Map stores computed results and transforms expensive O(2^n) operations into instant O(1) lookups.
analogy: A cache is like writing answers in the margin of a math test — the first time you compute 7x8, you write 56. The next time you need it, you look at the margin instead of recalculating. Each cached result saves you from repeating work you've already done.
try_it: Add a `cache_stats` function that reports how many computations were new vs cached. Add a counter that increments on every cache miss (new computation). Compare `cached_fib(30)` cache misses vs total calls. Then write `cached_is_prime` using a Map[Int, Bool] cache — once you know 17 is prime, never compute it again.
tips: Always check the cache BEFORE computing — that's the whole point: avoid unnecessary work
Cache the result immediately after computing — if you forget to `.insert()` the cache is useless
The cache key must uniquely identify the computation — `n` for fib(n), `(a,b)` for add(a,b)
common_mistakes: Forgetting to pass `&mut cache` — caching requires mutating the Map, so the reference must be mutable
Checking cache as `cache.get(&n)` without `contains` — both work, but `contains` is clearer for 'does it exist?'
Not caching the base case — even `fib(0)` and `fib(1)` should be cached, or you'll recompute them repeatedly
